newsitem.title: USA: U.S. housing starts reach lowest levels since '95.
newsitem.headline: U.S. housing starts reach lowest levels since '95.

text.p: U.S. housing starts weakened for the second consecutive month in October, reaching their lowest levels in over a year, U.S. economists said.

"With mortgage rates reaching peak levels in July, we kept waiting and waiting for them to break and for housing construction to break in response," said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
"It took longer than we thought, but it finally hit us here in the last two months, with single family starts in particular" falling to a 16-month trough, she added.
The U.S. Commerce Department reported a 5.1 percent decline in housing starts to a 1.37 million annual rate.
In September housing starts dropped 6.1 percent to a 1.440 million rate, Commerce said.

"This softening in housing starts has finally come into line with what the National Association of Home Builders has been reporting for several months...that their business is slowing," Nomura's Stone added.
U.S. experts agree that the weaker reports indicate that housing starts have probably capped for this cycle.
"October saw a 5.1 percent decline in starts. This is the first time we've been below 1.4 million units in a year," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities.
"The interest rate-sensitive sectors are starting to slacken off somewhat, reinforcing the message that the Federal Reserve had no need to change policy," Leahey added.

Meanwhile, with mortgage rates easing in the last few months, economists expect this will prevent the housing market from seeing steep declines, though they warned they do not expect much growth, either.
"People who buy homes are still concerned about heavy debt loads and high debt service costs...I think this is going to keep the housing sector from bouncing back," said Carol Stone.
"I think we'll see a fairly flat trend in the housing sector," Stone added."
